Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Akua had always found solace in the vast expanse of nature as a Park Ranger. She spent her days hiking through trails, leading groups of school children on educational tours, and ensuring the preservation of the park's delicate ecosystem. But all of that changed when her husband, Kwame, passed away suddenly in his sleep. Akua was consumed by grief and found herself unable to shake off the feeling of being "on edge" all the time. As she navigated the early days of her bereavement, Akua began to notice strange fragments of memories from the night Kwame died. She would be driving home from work when suddenly, without warning, she'd recall the sound of Kwame's alarm blaring in their bedroom, or the feeling of his cold skin as she touched his face. These sudden pieces of memory would leave her gasping for breath, her heart racing with a mix of fear and sadness. She couldn't explain why these memories came to her like photographs, vivid and unbidden, but they left her reeling. Akua's grief was overwhelming when these memories surfaced, often leaving her feeling emotionally numb and "dead inside." She struggled to connect with the world around her, even with her colleagues at the park. Simple tasks, like leading a nature walk or responding to visitor queries, felt like insurmountable challenges. Akua began to feel that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her as a Park Ranger and as Kwame's partner. In an attempt to cope with these feelings, Akua started taking on less responsibility at work, giving up her role in leading educational programs and instead focusing on more mundane tasks like maintenance and administration. She told herself it was safer this way, that she couldn't handle the stress of being "on" all the time. At home, she kept her mind occupied with endless cleaning and organizing, avoiding any moments of relaxation or quiet contemplation. But even these distractions didn't shield Akua from her body's constant state of tension. She'd catch herself scanning her surroundings for potential threats, her senses on high alert as if waiting for the next terrible thing to happen. At night, she'd lie awake, her mind racing with worst-case scenarios and memories of Kwame. Sleep became a luxury she couldn't afford. Akua knew that her husband's death had changed her permanently, that she was no longer the same person she used to be. She felt like she was living in a state of suspended animation, unable to move forward or find meaning in a world without Kwame. Her emotions were a jumble of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame – a toxic mix that left her feeling lost and alone. It's been months since Kwame's passing, but Akua still can't shake off the feeling that she's living on borrowed time. She knows that her loved ones are worried about her, that they're urging her to seek help. But what if therapy just makes things worse? What if it forces her to confront all these painful memories and emotions head-on? The thought of facing her grief in such a direct way terrifies Akua, but she's starting to realize that she can't keep living like this – constantly on edge, avoiding life itself. Perhaps, just perhaps, seeking help will be the first step towards finding a way out of this darkness.
